content.title: About
content.content: Beef heart is a dense, lean muscle from cattle, with a firm texture and a mild, beefy flavor that is similar to steak. It is classed as an organ meat, though it is a working muscle. Beef heart is eaten in many cuisines, grilled, braised, or stewed, and is used in dishes such as Peruvian anticuchos.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef heart is a muscle, so its taste and texture are closer to lean steak than to other organ meats.
It is very lean and can become tough if overcooked.
It naturally contains coenzyme Q10, a compound involved in cellular energy production.
Beef heart is used in Peruvian anticuchos, stews, and ground meat blends.
It is usually trimmed of fat, valves, and connective tissue before cooking.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef heart provides complete protein with relatively little fat.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12 and riboflavin
items.content: These vitamins support red blood cell formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron, zinc, and selenium
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport, immune function, and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Contains coenzyme Q10
items.content: Beef heart is a natural food source of coenzyme Q10.

items.title: Contains copper and niacin
items.content: These nutrients support metabolism.

items.title: Cholesterol and purines
items.content: Beef heart contains cholesterol and purines, which matters for people with gout or certain heart-related conditions.

items.title: Toughness when overcooked
items.content: Beef heart becomes dry and tough if overcooked, so cook it quickly over high heat or slowly with moisture.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Cook beef heart thoroughly, to at least about 71 °C (160 °F) for ground heart, and handle it hygienically.

items.title: Red meat consumption
items.content: Health organizations generally suggest moderating red meat, including organ meats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef heart can be trimmed, sliced thinly, and grilled or pan-seared quickly, marinated for skewers, or braised slowly in stews until tender. It can also be ground and mixed with other meat. Marinating helps keep it tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw beef heart in the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days, or freeze it for longer storage. Cooked heart should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days. Thaw frozen heart in the refrigerator.

classic-mixed-vegetables-frozen-cooked-n.title: Classic mixed vegetables, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Classic frozen mixed vegetables (broccoli, carrots, cauliflower, green peas) are ready to eat without added fat. They heat quickly in the microwave or on the stovetop while retaining most of their vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables are flash‑frozen right after harvest, preserving freshness and nutrients.
The blend typically contains 100 % vegetables with no added salt, sugar, or preservatives.
One serving provides about 5 % of the daily value for vitamin C.
Broccoli in the mix is rich in glucosinolates, compounds with antioxidant properties.
Frozen vegetables are often cheaper than fresh ones, yet can be nutritionally superior.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: The mix supplies vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, potassium and magnesium, supporting immunity and overall function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Vegetables are low in calories, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Broccoli and cauliflower contain glucosinolates that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Low sodium and no added fats favor healthy blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Allergy to individual vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to broccoli, cauliflower, or peas.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Broccoli and related vegetables contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

items.title: Texture loss if overcooked
items.content: Excessive heating can make the vegetables mushy and watery.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the mix in the microwave (2‑3 minutes) or sauté in a pan with a splash of water. Serve as a side dish, add to soups, stews, or pasta. Season with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C. After opening, use within 6‑12 months. Do not thaw and store at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Pecans are the edible seeds of the pecan tree (Carya illinoinensis), native to North America. The honey roasted version is coated with a thin layer of caramelized honey, giving the nuts a sweet aroma and a crunchy texture. Pecans are enjoyed raw, roasted, and are used in baking, desserts, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pecans belong to the hickory family and are more closely related to chestnuts than to walnuts.
Archaeological evidence suggests that Native American tribes domesticated pecans over 4,000 years ago.
The United States is the world’s largest pecan producer, especially the state of Georgia.
Honey roasted pecans are a common ingredient in the classic American pecan pie.
Pecans are a rich source of phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Pecans provide a notable amount of vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fat in pecans is monounsaturated, which can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in pecans supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: These nuts deliver plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc is essential for immune function and metabolism, and pecans are a good source.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pecans can trigger allergic reactions, including severe anaphylaxis, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Pecans are calorie-dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole pecans may pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Pecans contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in predisposed persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Honey roasted pecans make a convenient snack, can be added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or desserts. Lightly re‑roasting them in the oven can enhance their flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pecans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid. Discard nuts with a stale or rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato tots are small bite‑size pieces of potato made from fresh, fried or baked potatoes. They have a crispy golden exterior and a soft interior. Tots are commonly served as a snack, side dish, or fast‑food item.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato tots originated in the United States in the 1950s as an alternative to traditional potato wedges.
Traditionally, tots are formed from grated potato mixed with a little flour and seasoning.
There are three main cooking methods: deep‑frying, oven‑baking, and pan‑searing.
In many countries tots are served with cheese sauce, barbecue sauce, or sour cream dip.
Because they are small, tots are conveniently packaged in single‑serve bags for quick snacking.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potato batter retains vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Tots provide a quick source of carbohydrates, useful for active people and children.

items.title: Low sodium (when baked)
items.content: Baked tots can be prepared without added salt, making them more suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: If whole‑potato or vegetable additions are used in the mix, tots can supply a modest amount of dietary fiber.

items.title: High calorie density when fried
items.content: Fried tots contain a lot of fat and calories, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to potatoes, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound. Baking reduces its formation.

items.title: Salt and seasoning
items.content: Excessive salt in the finished product may be undesirable for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tots can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with dips (ketchup, cheese sauce, barbecue), added to salads, burgers, or used as a side dish for meat entrees.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tots in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Frozen tots stay fresh for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for any off‑flavors indicating rancidity.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat plain tortilla chips are crisp slices made from corn tortillas that are baked with less oil than traditional chips. They have a neutral flavor, making them a versatile snack and a base for a variety of dips and toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortilla chips originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a corn‑based alternative to potato chips.
The lower fat content is achieved by baking instead of deep‑frying.
They often appear in diet menus because they contain roughly 30 % fewer calories than regular chips.
Corn tortillas are naturally gluten‑free and high in fiber.
Tortilla chips are commonly served with guacamole, salsa, or yogurt‑based dips.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Less added oil makes them more suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The corn base provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and can help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Made from pure corn, they are safe for people with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Low sodium (when unsalted)
items.content: Unsalted versions help control overall sodium intake.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn and should avoid the product.

items.title: Sodium in flavored versions
items.content: Seasoned varieties can contain significant amounts of salt.

items.title: Caloric density remains
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the snack is still energy‑dense and should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy them straight from the bag, use as a crunchy base for toppings, add to salads, soups, or make chip‑tartare. They pair well with guacamole, salsa, hummus, or yogurt dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks to retain crispness and flavor. Discard if you notice off‑flavors or signs of rancidity.
